claims: The Julian calendar celebrated New Year's Day at the end of March/beginning of April.
The Gregorian calendar moved New Year's Day to January 1.
In 1564 (or 1582, according to popular lore), France shifted from the Julian calendar to the Gregorian calendar.
Due to slow communication or refusal to accept the change, many continued to celebrate the New Year on April 1.
These individuals were mocked as "April fools".
Victims of these tricks were called poisson d'avril (April fish).
"poisson d'avril" is a phrase still used in France today.
The ancient Roman festival of Hilaria was celebrated at the end of March by worshippers of Cybele.
Hilaria featured masquerades and disguises.
The vernal equinox marks the start of spring in the Northern Hemisphere.
The vernal equinox is in late March.
Chaucer's Canterbury Tales dates to 1392.
Some scholars suggest an early, ambiguous reference in "The Nun’s Priest’s Tale," which mentions pranks taking place 32 days after the start of March, placing it on April 1.
A poem by Flemish writer Eduard de Dene from 1561 describes a nobleman sending a servant on pointless "fool's errands" on April 1.
On April 1, 1698, pranksters convinced people to visit the Tower of London to "see the Lions washed".
In Scotland, April Fools' Day was a two-day event known as Huntigowk Day.
Huntigowk Day is named after the "gowk" (cuckoo bird), a symbol for a fool.
Huntigowk Day involved sending people on phony errands ("hunt the gowk").
In France, pranksters tape paper fish onto victims' backs in a "Poisson d'Avril" tradition.
In Scotland/England, Tailie Day involved placing "kick me" signs or fake tails on people.
